title: Why law firm invoices go unpaid, and how to chase them on a Mac in 2026

description: Why law firm invoices go unpaid: the causes, the cost in cash and time, and free fixes for Mac lawyers. Includes a 30, 60, 90 day routine.

intro: Law firm invoices go unpaid for three main reasons. Nobody owns collections, nobody follows up at 30, 60 or 90 days, and the bill itself can be late or unclear. This guide covers what it costs, why it happens, and fixes you can start this week on your Mac without buying anything.
tldr: Benchmarks range from 84% to 93% of billed amounts, depending on the year and the size of the firm.
Stuck balances often trace back to no owner, no 30, 60 and 90 day steps, and unclear bills.
Reminders help, but a UK survey suggests they do not cut late payment on their own.
Free fixes: name an owner, write the steps down, keep one tracker, and check the bill before it goes out.
Lazur explains settings, points at them, guides you one click at a time and drafts text. It does not send anything for you.

blocks.text: What unpaid invoices cost a law firm

The clearest recent benchmark comes from Clio's 2025 figures, as restated by Purpose in Action. The average law firm collection rate is 93%. The median collection lockup is 32 days, which is the time from invoice to payment. The median total lockup is 93 days, from work performed to cash. Put those together and the industry banks roughly 82 cents of each dollar of work it does, according to that summary.

A few points sound small. They are not. Purpose in Action gives a worked example. A firm invoices £250,000 a quarter and collects £212,500. That is an 85% collection rate, eight points below the 93% average. The gap is worth about £80,000 a year. Run the same sum with your own billed total and your own collection rate. If you do not track a collection rate yet, that is your first job.
Benchmarks disagree, so read them with care

Older and newer numbers do not line up. Clio's 2018 report, cited by the ABA Journal, shows an average collection rate of about 85%. The 2024 report for mid-sized firms, summarized by LawFuel, shows 84%. The 2025 figure is 93%. These come from different years and different firm sizes. Do not read them as one trend. The 2025 numbers also reach you second-hand, because Clio's own report could not be opened during research.

rows: Older data. Use it as a baseline only.

blocks.text: Vendor surveys give a rougher picture. CollBox surveyed 50 law firms about cash flow and published the results in June 2025. It found average outstanding invoices of about $206,000 per firm. Forty-one percent had invoices 90 or more days past due. Another 26% had invoices that were 60 to 90 days old. CollBox does not explain how it picked firms, so treat these as signals, not measurements.
Why invoices sit unpaid: the main causes
Purpose in Action names four causes of weak collection. Each one is a process gap, not a character flaw. Read the list and check which ones match your firm. You may find more than one at work.

items: No owner for collections. When everyone is responsible, nobody is.
Partner discomfort. Many partners would rather not ask for money, so the follow-up waits.
No cadence or escalation at 30, 60 or 90 days. The first reminder becomes the only reminder.
Billing delay and vague bills. Clients pay for work they have largely forgotten.

blocks.text: The billing side matters too. The ABA Journal says vague invoices and nonspecific billing for chunks of hours invite client questions. Those questions delay payment. Inaccurate timekeeping leads to inaccurate invoices, and those also delay payment. A client who has to ask what a line means has a reason to wait.

Reminders alone may not be enough. A UK government survey of small businesses, summarized by Innovation Growth Lab, found that 76% of businesses contact late-paying customers. The same summary says this does not appear to reduce late payments. It also found that 59% do not check a customer's payment record before they agree terms. These are UK small business figures, not law firm data. They still point at the same gap between chasing and checking.
Fixes you can use this week without buying anything

Start with ownership, because nothing else sticks without it. Choose one person who reviews every open invoice each week. Write that name on the matter opening sheet. Name a backup for holidays and busy months. You do not need new software for this. You need a name and a calendar slot.
Write a 30, 60, 90 day routine

The 30, 60 and 90 day marks are natural points for a step. Purpose in Action names the missing cadence as a cause. Write the steps down once, then follow them every month. Here is a simple version. At 30 days past due, send a short, polite email with the invoice attached. At 60 days, call the billing contact and confirm they received the bill. At 90 days, the responsible partner makes a direct call, then follows up in writing.

blocks.title: Keep it boring
blocks.text: Use the same day each week, the same three steps and the same owner. A routine you run every week beats a plan you review once a quarter.
Clean up the invoice before it goes out

Check the bill before it leaves. Replace one line that says legal services with task descriptions that name the work and the date. Show the matter number, the billing period and the person who did the work. Fix timekeeping every week, not at month end. Late time entries produce late, unclear invoices.

items: Sending the bill to the person who hired you, not the person who approves payment.
Waiting for a balance to age before anyone looks at it.
Sending a reminder with no invoice number or amount, so the client has to search for it.
Running reminders with no partner step, so the balance never reaches someone who can act.

blocks.text: Ask who pays before the first bill goes out. Confirm the approval route, the invoice contact and the payment method in the engagement letter. Ask how the client approves invoices internally. This takes a few minutes at intake and saves weeks later.

Keep one tracker. A spreadsheet is enough. Use columns for client, matter, invoice number, amount, sent date, due date, last contact, next step and owner. Sort by due date every Monday. You can run Google Sheets in Chrome on a Mac, or use Apple's Numbers. If a formula or menu stumps you, [Google Sheets help for Mac](/apps/google-sheets) covers the basics.
Automated reminders in billing tools you may already own

If you take card payments through LawPay, reminders live in its settings. The help center path is Settings > Client Billing > Billing and Invoice Preferences > Edit Preferences. Turn on the Automated Reminder toggle for each invoice. Reminders send only when an invoice has a due date and an open balance, and only to the invoice contact. Emails go out at 4 a.m. and texts at 8 a.m., based on the invoice creator's time zone. The article does not say whether reminders stop once an invoice is paid, so test that on one invoice. LawPay has two help center versions with different menu labels, so check against your own account.

QuickBooks Desktop for Mac also has payment reminders. Intuit lists QuickBooks Desktop Mac Plus as supported for automated payment reminders on invoices and statements. Schedule them from Customers > Payment Reminders > Schedule Payment Reminders. You can review and approve them before they go out. You can also send them later from Review & Send Payment Reminders. Confirm your version supports this before you rely on it.

TimeNet Law is a native macOS app, not a browser tool. The vendor describes billing, time capture and IOLTA-compliant three-way trust reconciliation. It lists a one-time price of $479.99 per user, or an optional $39.99 per user per month subscription. The minimum macOS version was not listed on the page reviewed. Check the vendor's pricing page before you buy.

blocks.title: Client data and firm rules
blocks.text: Invoices hold client names, matter details and sometimes case facts. Before you paste or dictate any of it into a tool, follow your employer's rules on client data. If your firm has not approved a tool, do not use it for client invoices.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and it answers out loud. It can point at things, so you find a reminder setting faster. It can also guide you one click at a time, waiting for each click. It does not click for you. It does not send invoices or emails for you.

Dictation is a separate feature. Hold fn and speak, and clean, formatted text appears at the cursor in any app. That helps when you need a firm-approved past-due note in Apple Mail or Outlook. Read every word before you send. Lazur drafts text, but you choose what goes out.

Here is a realistic moment. You open LawPay's billing preferences and cannot find the reminder toggle. Hold ⌥⌘ and ask where it is. Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Then ask for the next step, and click it yourself. The routine stays in your hands, and so does the decision.

Everyday actions help with the routine. Lazur can add a dated item to Apple Reminders by voice, so the 60 day call has a date and a reminder. Calendar events work the same way. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs and returns a summary and a report. That suits public pages about late payment rules. It does not replace your firm's own billing records.

Privacy comes first. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. faq.question: Why do law firm invoices go unpaid most often?
faq.answer: Three process gaps cause most of the delay. Nobody owns the balance, nobody follows up at set points, and the bill itself can be late or unclear. Purpose in Action and the ABA Journal both point to these causes. Most of the fixes cost time, not money.

faq.question: What is a normal law firm collection rate?
faq.answer: The sources disagree. Clio's 2018 figure was about 85%, the 2024 figure for mid-sized firms was 84%, and the 2025 figure is 93%. Use them as rough reference points. Compare against your own collection rate over the same period.

faq.question: Do automated payment reminders fix late payment?
faq.answer: They help with consistency. A UK survey of small businesses found that contacting late payers did not appear to reduce late payments. Pair reminders with a named owner and set 30, 60 and 90 day steps that a person follows.

faq.question: Does Lazur send reminders or invoices for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. It explains settings, points at them, guides you one click at a time, and drafts or dictates text. You read and send everything yourself.

faq.question: Can I paste client invoices into Lazur?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your employer's rules on client data still apply, so check them first.

faq.question: Does QuickBooks Desktop work for law firm billing on a Mac?
faq.answer: Intuit lists QuickBooks Desktop Mac Plus as supported for automated payment reminders on invoices and statements. Whether it fits your matter and trust records is a separate question. Ask your firm's accounting lead before you rely on it.

faq.question: What about TimeNet Law?
faq.answer: TimeNet Law is a native macOS app with billing, time capture and IOLTA-compliant three-way trust reconciliation, according to its vendor. The vendor lists $479.99 per user one time, or $39.99 per user per month. The minimum macOS version was not listed on the page reviewed. Check their pricing page.

costs.title: Cash you already earned
costs.text: Clio's 2025 figures put the median time from work performed to cash at 93 days. The collection step alone takes a median of 32 days. Those numbers come through a consultancy summary, so treat them as a guide. Run your own numbers before you set any target for your firm.

costs.title: Money lost to the gap
costs.text: Purpose in Action's worked example uses a firm that bills £250,000 a quarter and collects £212,500. That 85% collection rate sits eight points below the 93% average. The summary puts the gap at about £80,000 a year. Use your own billed total and your own collection rate to find your gap.

costs.title: Time spent chasing
costs.text: CollBox found that chasing past-due bills is the top accounts receivable challenge, cited by 35% of the firms it surveyed. The survey did not measure how many hours that takes. Track your own chasing time for a few weeks, then decide what it is worth to you.

costs.title: Cash flow on the next matter
costs.text: Late payment pushes back every other bill. Money you are owed can end up paying for rent, staff and software that you already committed to. You do not need a survey to see that effect. Check it in your own bank account each month.

causes.title: No owner for collections
causes.text: When a balance has no owner, everybody assumes someone else is chasing it. Purpose in Action names missing ownership as a core cause of low collection. The fix is one named person who reviews every open balance each week, with a backup for busy months.

causes.title: Partner discomfort with chasing money
causes.text: Many partners would rather not ask a client for money. Purpose in Action names partner discomfort as a cause of weak collection. The fix is a clear split of labor, so the partner makes one well-timed call instead of a series of vague nudges that never land.

causes.title: No cadence or escalation
causes.text: A reminder that goes out once, then never again, teaches the client to wait. Purpose in Action names the absence of a 30, 60 and 90 day cadence as a cause. Without steps at those marks, nothing changes when a balance gets older.

causes.title: Billing delay and vague bills
causes.text: Clients pay for work they have largely forgotten, so a late bill tends to wait. The ABA Journal says vague invoices and nonspecific billing for chunks of hours invite client questions, and those questions delay payment. Inaccurate timekeeping leads to inaccurate invoices.

causes.title: Payment terms that nobody checked
causes.text: A UK government survey of small businesses found that 59% do not check a customer's payment record before they agree to a contract, according to an Innovation Growth Lab summary. Law firms were not in that survey. The lesson still applies. Ask how a new client has paid before you take the matter.

fixes.title: Name one owner and a backup
fixes.text: Choose one person who reviews every open invoice each week. Write the name on the matter opening sheet and the tracker. Name a backup for holidays and busy months. Without a name, every other fix has no one to carry it out.

fixes.title: Check the bill before it leaves
fixes.text: Replace one-line descriptions with task descriptions that name the work and the date. Add the matter number, the billing period and the person who did the work. Fix timekeeping every week. Late entries produce late and unclear invoices, which slow payment.

fixes.title: Confirm who pays at intake
fixes.text: Put the approval route, the invoice contact and the payment method in the engagement letter. Ask how the client approves invoices internally. Fixing this on the first bill is far easier than chasing a stalled approval on the fortieth.

fixes.title: Keep one tracker with a next step on every line
fixes.text: Use one shared sheet with client, matter, invoice number, amount, due date, last contact, next step and owner. A line without a next step is a line nobody is working. Sort by due date each Monday and review the top rows first.

fixes.title: Test reminders before you trust them
fixes.text: If your billing tool has automated reminders, test them on one internal invoice. Confirm the timing, the recipient and whether reminders stop after payment. LawPay and QuickBooks Desktop both document their settings, but the menu names can differ by version.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: List every open invoice past 30 days
plan.text: Pull the aging report from your billing tool or your accounts. Sort by days past due. Note the responsible partner on each matter. Add up the total owed. That total is your starting point for the rest of the plan.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Name one owner and a backup
plan.text: Put one name on the collection list. Add a backup for holidays and busy weeks. Write the owner on the matter opening sheet, so every new matter starts with a named person.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Build the tracker
plan.text: Create one shared sheet with client, matter, invoice number, amount, due date, last contact, next step and owner. Enter every open invoice. Add a next step and a date to each line.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Set up and test reminders
plan.text: Turn on automated reminders in your billing tool if you have one. Test on one internal invoice first. Confirm the timing, the recipient and whether reminders stop after payment.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Agree the 30, 60, 90 steps
plan.text: Meet the responsible partner for a short session. Agree who makes the 60 day call and who makes the 90 day call. Write the steps into the tracker so they survive the next busy month.

plan.label: Week 2
plan.title: Check the next bill before it goes out
plan.text: Before the next invoice leaves, check the narrative, the timekeeping and the named approver. Send it once it passes that check. Then repeat the check on every bill.
